items.title: Fable 5.1 (Fully Tested & Real cost comparisons): It's A GREAT Model but there's still ONE ISSUE!
items.summary:
Visit Verdent: https://www.verdent.ai/?id=700712
Visit AISeeKing (my second channel with more cool ai stuff): https://www.youtube.com/@aiseeking


In this video, I’ll be reviewing the new Claude Fable 5.1 model, covering its benchmarks, API pricing, cache savings, coding performance, safety changes, and real-world limitations. I’ll also test it across eight KingBench tasks to see how it compares with Fable 5, Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GLM 5.3, and other leading AI models.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Claude Fable 5.1 delivers major improvements in coding, frontend development, 3D generation, and long-horizon agentic tasks.
🏆 It scored 74 out of 80, or 92.5 percent, on KingBench—the highest score achieved by any model tested so far.
⌚ Fable 5.1 set a new record on the difficult 3D wristwatch task, improving from Fable 5’s score of 4 to an impressive 9 out of 10.
💸 API pricing remains at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, while cache-read pricing has been reduced by 75 p

Now, let me show you what all of this actually cost because I pulled up the usage screen after all the tests. Total cost for the whole session was $3.60. 60s. There's also a tiny Hiku 4.5 line with 956 input tokens, which is just Claude codes helper stuff. If you do the math, the 22.9,000 output tokens are about 1 by15s. That's a 20% saving, which lines up with the 25% typical number. Anthropic is quoting. For the plan side, this session used 21% of my session limit, 5% of my weekly limit across all models, and 9% of my weekly fable limit. And there's a plus 50% weekly limits promo running through September 13th. Now, let's come to the thoughts portion. And I've been reading through Hacker News X and a few outlets to see what other people are finding. The biggest complaint is about cash rights. One of the more detailed real world breakdowns that's going around shows Fable 5.1 generating 4.39 million output tokens out of 573 million total tokens on a bill of $1,023.78. Cash reads were 89.8% of the tokens, but only 12.6% of the cost at $128.67. Cash rights were 9.4% of the tokens, but 65.8% of the cost at $67,387. Output was 21.4% at $21929. So, the cash rate cut is great, but the bill is now dominated by cash rights, which didn't move at all, and my own session shows the exact same shape at a much smaller scale with cash rights at around 58%. There's also a fair point being made that the price cut only applies to paper token billing and does nothing for subscription users. The second big theme is refusals. And this one is weird. Anthropic says 60% fewer cyber interventions. And I believe that number is real, but the failure mode when it does trigger is strange. People are reporting that Fable will happily write unsafe Win32 Rust code and then refuse to review the exact same code as potentially dangerous. Just mentioning Lennux CMP is getting flagged for some people. And one estimate floating around is that roughly 80% of what someone intended to send to Fable actually got silently routed to Opus because of the alignment classifier, especially for anything networking related. So if you're doing low-level systems or security work, you might be paying Fable prices and getting Opus answers without knowing. There's also a funny one where Fable basically gas lit itself. It assumed it had permission on a private server for a reverse engineering task, and once it believed that it did work, it had refused a minute earlier. So the safety layer is more about what it thinks the context is than what you're actually asking. The third theme is the anti-distillation stuff. All three breaking changes patch the same thing, which is people extracting raw chain of thought by giving the model a fake tool or having haiku repeat another model's thinking blocks. The general read is that at least half the changes in this release are anti-distillation strategies. Some people are calling the model useless without visible thought traces. That's a bit harsh, but if you were relying on reading the reasoning, that's now behind a progress updates beta that only shows status lines. Then there's the writing style, and this is one Anthropic's own docs. Admit to the migration guide literally lists denser sentences, fewer paragraph breaks, less bold headers, and unmarked quotations and summaries as known behavior differences. The common complaint is that the pros is denser and exhausting to read, even though there are fewer stock phrases, and that the documentation it writes is choppy and long and lacks flow. So, it writes less like an AI and more like a tired engineer, which some people like and some really don't. The docs also list a few agentic quirks that I found interesting. It sometimes issues one tool call per turn instead of batching, so it can feel slower. It gives fewer progress updates during long runs. On low effort, it answers from memory instead of searching. And it does whole file rewrites instead of targeted edits more often, which costs you more output tokens for small changes. That last one is worth remembering when you look at the cachite number. On the positive side, the Clawed Code team is saying it's the best model they have for coding, data analysis, computer use, and long agentic work. That it gets a lot further into a long task before it needs your input, and that it's better at telling you when it's stuck. People doing long planning heavy work are saying it's great at planning complex problems with verification steps and that they rarely hit the security downgrade. One team measured about a 30% real cost reduction versus Fable 5 on their evals. And at 95% cache hit rates, the sweet spot for context size roughly doubles from 200,000 to 400,000 tokens. On code review, one eval ran it on 45 code review tasks with 105 known issues. Recall was basically flat at 61% versus 61.9 for Fable 5, but precision went from 32.8 to 37.3%. Total comments dropped 34% and nitpicks dropped 70%. The catch is reviews took 49% longer and turning effort up to high actually made recall worse at 57.1%. So more thinking did not help there. And one more thing that I found a bit odd. Anthropic themselves now say Opus 5 should be the default and you should reserve Fable 5.1 for demanding reasoning and long horizon agentic work. A good chunk of people agree saying Opus 5 is better than Fable for everything except creative programming work and that they saw minimal tangible improvements for double the cost. Now quickly on where I'll actually be using this. I'll be running Fable 5.1 through Verdant for my day-to-day work and this release is a pretty good fit for it. Verdant is the parallel agent tool I use where each task runs in its own isolated work tree and you can have a bunch of agents going at once while it keeps you posted on what's done. And that's exactly the kind of long multi-step agentic workload where the 75% cheaper cache reads actually show up because the model keeps rereading the same big prefix on every turn. Plus, Verdant doesn't nerf the models and it supports bring your own key so you can plug your own anthropic key in and pay API rates directly if you'd rather do that. I'll have a proper video on Fable 5.1 in Verdant with a few parallel projects soon. So, what's the verdict? If you ask me on my bench, this is the best model I have ever tested, and it's not close. 92.5%. First model above 90, and it broke the wristwatch question that nothing else could do. The Movie Tracker app was also flawless. It's not perfect, though. The bow and arrow game is still just an eight. The contact lens case dropped a point and the real world complaints about cashright costs, silent opus fallback on security work and the denser writing are all legit. But the front end and 3D work is on another level. The long horizon stuff is rock solid. And if you're on a max plan with the 50% fable allowance, a session like mine that costs $3.60 on the API barely dents your weekly limit. If you're on API and doing short calls, you're paying the same as Fable 5 for a 2 to 5 point gain. If you're doing long agent sessions, you're paying 20 to 45% less for the best model out there. That's where it makes sense. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments.
